parts:
Hi group,

Rookie SCR modeler here. I've switched over from JAGS to oSCR to help deal with the computation time for SCR modelling over a discrete state space with camera trap data, but I'm still finding that my run times for even the most basic models in oSCR take a very long time. I'm not sure if this is due to the nature of my dataset or if there's an error in my model structure that I'm missing.

I'm working with a very reduced dataset - using a subset with 8 individuals, 40 cameras, and 30 occasions (days), whereas the full dataset uses 103 cameras and over a year of trap-days. However, even with this reduced dataset, the null model (D~1, p0~1, sigma~1) takes 58 minutes to run. When I use the full dataset the null model takes over 2 days to run. I just thought it would be running much faster so this seems a little weird to me. It's occurred to me that this might be because I have a large number of pixels in the state space (11550), but as it's already at a resolution of 250m * 250m, I'm reluctant to go coarser than that for the purposes of this project. 

Anyway, eventually I'll need to be using the full dataset doing a model selection process with up to 6 spatial covariates. Given the current state of things it's looking like this could take forever to accomplish, which isn't the end of the world, but any thoughts or suggestions on improving processing time would be very much appreciated! Or if anyone is able to spot an error in the structure that I may have missed.

I bet its that 4th column. I have to admit, the binomial model probably needs some work, its not as up to date/as well tested as the Poisson model. Also, make sure you have the most recent version of the package (you can do that using the first few lines of code)

 

Hope this helps!!! 😊

 

install.packages("githubinstall")

install.packages("devtools")

library(githubinstall)

library(devtools)

 

#install oSCR directly from github

install_github("jaroyle/oSCR")

 

#load oSCR

library(oSCR)

 

edf <- read.csv("CV_grid_edf2_subset.csv")

 

#need to make day 90 occasion 1 - some sausage making:

days2occasion <- data.frame(day=90:119, occasion=1:length(90:119))

edf2 <- merge(edf,days2occasion,by="day",all.x=T, all.y = F)

head(edf2)

 

 

 

tdf <- read.csv("CV_grid_tdf_subset.csv")

head(tdf)

 

#remove the pixel ID column so its < ID X Y opperation1:K >

tdf <- tdf[,-4]

 

sf <- data2oscr(edf = edf2,

                sess.col = 2,

                id.col = 3,

                occ.col = 5,

                trap.col = 4,

                tdf = list(tdf),

                K = 30,

                ntraps = nrow(tdf))$scrFrame

 

ss <- make.ssDF(sf,buffer = 4, res=0.5)

 

par(mfrow=c(1,2))

plot(sf)

plot(ss,sf)

 

#set trimS to the same value as the buffer to speecd things up

system.time(m0 <- oSCR.fit(scrFrame=sf,ssDF=ss, trimS=4))

Hi Chris,

Amazing, thank you so much for your prompt suggestions. I adapted my script to match your changes - the biggest change was defining the state space data frame using the make.ssDF function (as opposed to importing pixel coordinates) and trimming the state space as an argument to the model fitting function. Even when keeping the 250m resolution the models run much faster, but I also reduced the resolution to 1km as Andy suggested which greatly improved run time as well. As a result I can run models the full dataset with spatial covariates in under 3 hours, which is orders of magnitude faster. So, it worked! Also good to know about the binomial models. 

Just wondering, I noticed that there is a huge jump in the AIC values (ie. >200) when the models incorporate any of the spatial covariates in the rsfDF. Is this really suggesting that the spatial covariates are not contributing to space use by this species, as compared to the null model and models with just behavioral variables like sex? Or does the addition of the RSF make it so that the models are not really comparable by AIC to models without spatial covariates? Hope that question is clear, but let me know if I can clarify.

Again thanks for your help, much appreciated!

Nina

Hello,

 

Key point is that you must be able to define a covariate for _every_ point in the ssDF.

If you have say a raster of come covariate you wish to use to describe density, say ‘cov.rast’, then for a single session state space, you could use the extract function in the raster package:

 

ssDF[[1]]$covariate <- extract(cov.rast,                                                                      

                               SpatialPoints(cbind(ssDF[[1]]$X, ssDF[[1]]$Y)))

 

 

oSCR has a helper function to do this too called ‘extract.rast()’. You supply a raster and an ssDF object and a few other arguments related to how you want the summary to be done. This is not documented up as I still need to do some better testing on it.

 

Chris

install.packages("githubinstall")

install.packages("devtools")

library(githubinstall)

library(devtools)

 

#install oSCR directly from github

install_github("jaroyle/oSCR")

 

#load oSCR

library(oSCR)

 

edf <- read.csv("CV_grid_edf2_subset.csv")

 

#need to make day 90 occasion 1 - some sausage making:

days2occasion <- data.frame(day=90:119, occasion=1:length(90:119))

edf2 <- merge(edf,days2occasion,by="day",all.x=T, all.y = F)

head(edf2)

 

 

 

tdf <- read.csv("CV_grid_tdf_subset.csv")

head(tdf)

 

#remove the pixel ID column so its < ID X Y opperation1:K >

tdf <- tdf[,-4]

 

sf <- data2oscr(edf = edf2,

                sess.col = 2,

                id.col = 3,

                occ.col = 5,

                trap.col = 4,

                tdf = list(tdf),

                K = 30,

                ntraps = nrow(tdf))$scrFrame

 

ss <- make.ssDF(sf,buffer = 4, res=0.5)

 

par(mfrow=c(1,2))

plot(sf)

plot(ss,sf)

 

#set trimS to the same value as the buffer to speecd things up

system.time(m0 <- oSCR.fit(scrFrame=sf,ssDF=ss, trimS=4))
